present.name: Present-tense endings
present.about: A verb's ending changes with who does it: hablo (I speak), hablas (you speak), habla (he or she speaks).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

present.short: A verb's ending says who does it: tomo (I drink), tomas (you drink), toma (he, she drinks), tomamos (we drink).

no-subject.name: No subject needed
no-subject.about: Spanish often leaves out subject words when the verb's ending makes the person clear, and weather verbs have no word for it: Hablo (I speak), Llueve (rains).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

no-subject.short: The ending already says who, so yo, tú and the rest are left out unless it matters who: Tomo café (I drink coffee).

gender.name: Gender and agreement
gender.about: Every noun is masculine or feminine, and the words with it match it: el libro nuevo, la casa nueva, las casas nuevas.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gender.short: Every noun is masculine (el, un) or feminine (la, una), and the words with it match: el libro, la mesa.

adjective-after.name: Adjectives after the noun
adjective-after.about: Most describing words come after the noun: una casa pequeña (a house small).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

adjective-after.short: Most describing words come after the noun and match it: una casa pequeña (a house small).

negation.name: no before the verb
negation.about: no goes right before the verb, and before any little pronoun in front of it: No lo sé (not it I know).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

negation.short: no goes right before the verb: No tomo café (I don't drink coffee).

question.name: Questions
question.about: A question opens with ¿ and closes with ?, and after a question word the subject usually follows the verb: ¿Dónde vive tu hermano? (where lives your brother).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

question.short: A question opens with ¿ and closes with ?; after a question word the verb comes next: ¿Dónde está el carro?

ser-estar.name: ser and estar
ser-estar.about: Spanish has two verbs for to be: ser for what someone or something is (and where an event takes place), estar for where a person or thing is and how they are: Es mi hermana (she is my sister), Está en casa (she is at home).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

ser-estar.short: estar says where something is and how someone is (está aquí, estoy bien); ser says what something is (es un libro).

hay.name: hay: there is, there are
hay.about: One word, hay, says both there is and there are: Hay dos baños (there are two bathrooms).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover there are too in revision 7 (the director, 2026-11-09).

hay.short: hay says there is and there are: Hay café (there's coffee), Hay dos baños (there are two bathrooms).

object-pronoun.name: Pronouns before the verb
object-pronoun.about: Little words for it, him, her, me, you and us (lo, la, me, te, nos) go before a conjugated verb: Lo veo (it I see). They attach to an infinitive or an affirmative command: verlo, míralo (but no lo mires).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover me, te and nos too in revision 7 (the director, 2026-11-09). Wording made true of every use in revision 7 (lx-langs-2, 2026-11-09).

object-pronoun.short: lo, la, me, te and nos go just before a conjugated verb: Lo veo (it I see), and attach to an infinitive: verlo.

personal-a.name: a before a person
personal-a.about: When the verb acts on a specific person (or a pet), a goes in front of them: Veo a mis padres (I see to my parents).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

personal-a.short: Put a before a specific person the verb acts on: Veo a mi mamá (I see to my mom).

gustar.name: gustar: liking
gustar.about: To like something, you say it pleases you: Me gusta el café (to me pleases the coffee), so the verb matches the thing you like.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gustar.short: To say you like something, say it pleases you: Me gusta el café (to me pleases the coffee).

reflexive.name: Reflexive verbs
reflexive.about: Some verbs come with me, te, se or nos before the verb, pointing back to whoever does it: Me levanto (myself I raise: I get up).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover nos too in revision 7 (the director, 2026-11-09).

reflexive.short: Some verbs take me, te, se or nos pointing back at who does it: Me levanto (myself I raise: I get up).

modal.name: Verb + infinitive
modal.about: After querer, poder, necesitar and tener que, the next verb is in its basic form, the infinitive: Quiero comer (I want to eat).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

modal.short: After querer, poder and tener que, the next verb stays in its basic form: Quiero comer (I want to eat).

ir-a.name: ir a: going to
ir-a.about: voy a, vas a, va a and an infinitive say what's going to happen: Voy a comer (I go to eat).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

ir-a.short: voy a, vas a, va a and a basic form say what's going to happen: Voy a comer (I go to eat).

pronoun-attached.name: Pronouns joined to the infinitive
pronoun-attached.about: With an infinitive, the little pronoun can join its end as one word: Quiero verte (I want to see-you).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

pronoun-attached.short: With a basic form, the little pronoun can join its end: Quiero verte (I want to see-you).

progressive.name: estar + -ando, -iendo: right now
progressive.about: estar with a verb ending in -ando or -iendo says what's in progress: Estoy comiendo (I am eating); estaba comiendo (I was eating).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover -iendo too in revision 7 (the director, 2026-11-09). Wording made true of every use in revision 7 (lx-langs-2, 2026-11-09).

progressive.short: estar with -ando or -iendo says what's in progress: Estoy comiendo (I am eating).

perfect.name: Present perfect: haber + participle
perfect.about: The present perfect puts a form of haber before the participle, and any little pronoun goes before haber: Lo he visto (it I have seen).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover every form of haber too in revision 7 (the director, 2026-11-09).

perfect.short: A form of haber and a participle: He comido (I have eaten); a little pronoun goes before haber.

past.name: Simple past
past.about: One word with its own ending says what happened and is over: Ayer comí paella (yesterday I ate paella).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

past.short: One word with its own ending says what happened and is over: Ayer comí (yesterday I ate).

tener.name: tener: I have hunger
tener.about: Where English says I'm hungry or I'm twenty, Spanish says I have: Tengo hambre (I have hunger), Tengo veinte años (I have twenty years).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover age, fear and having too in revision 7 (the director, 2026-11-09).

tener.short: Where English says I'm hungry or I'm twenty, Spanish says I have: Tengo hambre (I have hunger).

de.name: de: of
de.about: Spanish joins nouns with de where English puts one before the other: la estación de tren (the station of train), la casa de mis abuelos (the house of my grandparents).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

de.short: de joins nouns where English puts one before the other, and says whose: la llave del carro, es de mi mamá.

possessive.name: mi, tu, su: words for belonging
possessive.about: mi (my), tu (your), su (his, her, its, their, your formal) go before the noun and are the same for el and la words; with a plural noun they add -s: mi libro, mi llave, mis libros.

source.note: Added with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

possessive.short: mi, tu and su go before the noun, the same for el and la words: mi libro, mi llave (my book, my key).

demonstrative.name: esto, eso, este, ese: this and that
demonstrative.about: esto (this) and eso (that) point at a thing you don't name: ¿Qué es esto? (what is this?). este and ese go with a noun or stand for one, and match it: este libro, esa mesa, ese (that one).

source.note: Added with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.short: esto and eso point at a thing you don't name: ¿Qué es esto? (what is this?), Eso es un libro (that is a book).

usted.name: usted: polite you
usted.about: usted is the polite you, for someone you don't know or show respect to, and its verb takes the form for él and ella: ¿Usted sabe dónde está? (you know where it is?), Esto es para usted (this is for you).

source.note: Added with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

usted.short: usted is the polite you, and its verb takes the él and ella form: ¿Sabe usted dónde está? (know you where it is?).

question-word.name: Who, what, where?
question-word.about: Question words ask for missing information and carry written accents: qué (what), quién (who), dónde (where), cómo (how). Later add cuándo (when), cuánto (how much) and por qué (why).

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.short: qué asks what, quién asks who, dónde asks where and cómo asks how: ¿Cómo puedo ayudar?

plural.name: More than one
plural.about: Most nouns add -s after a vowel or -es after a consonant; final z changes to c before -es. Articles and describing words agree with the noun. A plural subject takes a plural verb.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.short: More than one cita is citas, and more than one hora is horas: dos citas, dos horas. Use las with feminine plural nouns.

contractions.name: al and del
contractions.about: The prepositions a and de join the article el: a + el = al, de + el = del. The pronoun él keeps its accent and stays separate: a él, de él.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

contractions.short: a + el becomes al, and de + el becomes del. Use al in ver al doctor. With la or las the words stay separate.

time-telling.name: Saying the time
time-telling.about: Use es la una for one o'clock and son las followed by the hour for other times. To say when something happens, use a la una or a las followed by the hour.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.short: Son las dos tells the time. A las dos says when: Mi cita es a las dos.

imperative.name: Giving instructions
imperative.about: An affirmative command to tú uses its command form: llama (call), espera (wait). Many regular forms look like the él or ella present form; common irregular commands must be learned separately. Object pronouns attach to affirmative commands, with a written accent when needed.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.short: Use an affirmative command to tell someone you call tú to act: Llama al doctor, por favor. Add por favor to make the request polite.

verb-preposition.name: A verb's partners
verb-preposition.about: Learn a verb with the words it takes after it. Spanish esperar directly takes what is awaited; a specific person usually needs personal a. English wait for does not require a Spanish word for for.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.short: Esperamos al doctor means we are waiting for the doctor. The a is personal a, and a + el becomes al.

prepositional-pronoun.name: Pronouns after prepositions
prepositional-pronoun.about: After most prepositions use mí for me and ti for you. With con these become conmigo and contigo. Other pronouns, such as él, ella and usted, keep their usual forms.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction. Short name made to cover mí and ti too in revision 7 (the director, 2026-11-09).

prepositional-pronoun.short: contigo means with you, addressing one person as tú: Quiero estar contigo. It is written as one word.

because.name: Giving a reason with porque
because.about: porque introduces a reason clause with its own conjugated verb. It is one word without an accent. It does not send the verb to the end of the clause.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

because.short: porque gives a reason: Me quedo en cama porque quiero dormir (I am staying in bed because I want to sleep).

negative-concord.name: Negatives working together
negative-concord.about: After the verb, nada, nadie, nunca and ningún normally combine with a preceding negative such as no. Before the verb, a negative word supplies the negation without no. These words express one negative meaning together.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

negative-concord.short: No tengo nada means I have nothing. No conozco a nadie means I do not know anyone. Before the verb, omit no: Nadie quiere trabajar hoy.

que-clause.name: What you think: creo que
que-clause.about: que links an introductory verb such as creer to the content of the thought. After affirmative creo que, the clause normally uses the indicative. The subordinate clause has its own conjugated verb; que is unaccented.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

que-clause.short: Creo que podemos comer aquí means I think we can eat here. Spanish uses que to introduce the thought, even when English omits that.

indirect-object.name: Who receives it
indirect-object.about: An indirect-object pronoun identifies the recipient of what is given or told: me, te, le, nos or les. Before a conjugated verb it is separate; it can attach to an infinitive. An a phrase can make the recipient explicit.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

indirect-object.short: Mi mamá me cuenta una historia means My mom is telling me a story. In Él le cuenta algo a mi amiga, le and a mi amiga name the same recipient.

por-para.name: Different uses of por and para
por-para.about: por and para overlap with English for but express different relations. para can identify a recipient or purpose; por can give a reason or introduce what someone goes to fetch. Learn the whole expression rather than replacing every English for with one preposition.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

por-para.short: Voy a traer agua para todos names the recipients. ¿Quieres ir por café? means Do you want to go get coffee? por introduces what is being fetched.

double-object.name: Giving it to someone
double-object.about: Put the recipient pronoun before the direct-object pronoun. Before lo, la, los or las, le and les become se: Se lo llevo a mi hermano. An a phrase can identify the recipient.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction.

double-object.short: The recipient comes first: se lo. Use se instead of le or les before lo, la, los or las; keep the pair together.

subjunctive.name: Command forms
subjunctive.about: Negative tú commands use present-subjunctive forms: no tires, no pongas. Commands addressed to usted or ustedes use present-subjunctive forms with or without no: ponga, no ponga; pongan, no pongan. These forms also have other uses, introduced later.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction. Short name made to cover what its tagged sentences do in revision 7 (lx-langs-2, 2026-11-09, lx-app's chip class).

subjunctive.short: Use present-subjunctive forms for negative tú commands and for usted/ustedes commands. Put object pronouns before a negative command: No lo pongas en la mesa.

quantity.name: A number without its noun
quantity.about: When the noun is understood, a number can stand alone: ¿Necesitas libros? Tengo dos. Use uno or una for one, and ninguno or ninguna for none, agreeing with the noun understood. Before a masculine singular noun, use un and ningún.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction.

quantity.short: A number can replace a known noun. uno/una and ninguno/ninguna agree with that noun; after the verb, none keeps no: No tengo ninguno.

infinitive-clause.name: An action as a unit
infinitive-clause.about: An infinitive can name the activity being described: Manejar es importante. It can follow a preposition required by the construction: tiempo para comer, difícil de entender. English to does not have one fixed Spanish equivalent.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction.

infinitive-clause.short: Use the infinitive for an activity: Manejar es importante. Learn the connecting word with the construction: tiempo para comer, difícil de entender.

si-clause.name: Open conditions with si
si-clause.about: si introduces a condition. For an open present or future condition, use the present indicative after si. The result can be a statement, a plan or a request: Si tienes tiempo, envíame la foto. si has no accent.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 81–100, open to correction. Short name made to cover what its tagged sentences do in revision 7 (lx-langs-2, 2026-11-09, lx-app's chip class).

si-clause.short: Use si plus the present for an open condition: Si tienes tiempo, envíame la foto (If you have time, send me the photo).

indirect-question.name: A question inside a sentence
indirect-question.about: An embedded question identifies something someone knows, asks or does not understand. Keep the written accent on question words such as dónde and qué. Use unaccented si for whether: No sé si ella vive aquí.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 81–100, open to correction.

indirect-question.short: Keep dónde, qué, cómo, cuándo and por qué accented inside a sentence. Use si without an accent for whether.

imperfect-subjunctive.name: Imagined situations with como si
imperfect-subjunctive.about: como si introduces an imagined comparison. Use the imperfect subjunctive for a situation simultaneous with the main clause: Parece como si ella viviera aquí. The -ra forms have equivalent -se forms in this use.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 81–100, open to correction.

imperfect-subjunctive.short: After como si, use the imperfect subjunctive for an imagined simultaneous situation: como si viviera aquí (as if she lived here).

future.name: The simple future
future.about: The simple future attaches endings to the infinitive or an irregular stem. It expresses predictions, promises and other future statements; it can also express a guess about the present. ir a plus an infinitive is another common future construction, and their uses overlap.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 101–120, open to correction.

future.short: Use the simple future for a future statement or promise: Mañana trabajaré en casa. ir keeps its infinitive in iré: I will go.

conditional.name: Would and polite requests
conditional.about: Conditional endings attach to the infinitive or the same irregular stems used for the simple future. The conditional expresses would and can soften a request. An imagined condition can use si plus the imperfect subjunctive with a conditional result: Si tuviera tiempo, iría contigo.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 101–120, open to correction.

conditional.short: Me gustaría means I would like. ¿Podrías ayudarme? softens a request. Si tuviera tiempo, iría contigo gives the result of an imagined condition.

relative.name: Describing which one
relative.about: A relative clause links a noun to a description: el libro que quiero. Spanish retains que where English can omit that. donde connects a place with what happens there: la ciudad donde vivo. These relative words have no written accent.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 101–120, open to correction.

relative.short: Use que to describe the named person or thing: el libro que quiero. Use donde for a place: la ciudad donde vivo.

imperfect.name: Past habits and background
imperfect.about: The imperfect presents past habits, states and ongoing background without presenting their boundaries as the focus. The preterite presents events as bounded. The choice depends on viewpoint, not simply on duration: Cuando llegué a casa, llovía.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 101–120, open to correction.

imperfect.short: Antes vivía en esta casa describes a past living situation. In Cuando llegué a casa, llovía, llegué is the completed arrival and llovía is the rain in progress.

subjunctive-time.name: When a future event happens
subjunctive-time.about: Use cuando plus the present subjunctive for an event still ahead: Cuando llegues, te llamo. The main clause can use a present form for a future plan, a future tense or a command. For a present habit or completed past event, cuando normally takes the indicative. The time clause can come first or last.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 121–140, open to correction.

subjunctive-time.short: Cuando llegues, te llamo means When you arrive, I will call you. Use the subjunctive in the future time clause, even though English uses an ordinary present form.

past-perfect.name: Had already done
past-perfect.about: The past perfect uses imperfect haber and an unchanged past participle to put an event before a past reference point: Cuando llegué, ella ya había salido. Context identifies the subject of había. Object pronouns go before haber.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 121–140, open to correction.

past-perfect.short: había, habías, habíamos or habían plus a participle says what had happened before a past reference point. The participle does not agree with the subject: ella había salido.

passive.name: What gets done
passive.about: ser plus an agreeing participle presents an action: El libro fue escrito por mi hermana. por can name the agent. Everyday passive se also focuses on what is done, with the verb agreeing with its subject: Se venden casas. estar plus a participle instead describes a state.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 141–160, open to correction.

passive.short: Use ser plus an agreeing participle for an action, or passive se with a verb agreeing with the thing affected: El libro fue escrito por mi hermana; Se venden casas.

comparative.name: Comparing things and people
comparative.about: Use más or menos with an adjective and que for unequal comparisons, and tan with an adjective and como for equal comparisons. The adjective agrees with what it describes. Later, learn mejor, peor, mayor and menor, and relative superlatives with an article plus más or menos.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 141–160, open to correction.

comparative.short: más ... que means more ... than, menos ... que means less ... than, and tan ... como means as ... as. Keep más, menos and tan unchanged; make the adjective agree.

impersonal-se.name: People in general
impersonal-se.about: Impersonal se leaves the people doing an action unnamed and uses a third-person singular verb: Aquí se habla español; ¿Se puede entrar? A specific human direct object has personal a and does not control verb agreement: Aquí se llama a los padres. Passive se instead has an agreeing subject.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 141–160, open to correction.

impersonal-se.short: Use se and a third-person singular verb to talk about people in general: Aquí se habla español. In Aquí se llama a los padres, los padres is a human object, not an agreeing subject.

accidental-se.name: Something happened to me
accidental-se.about: se followed by me, te, le, nos or les presents an event with someone affected: Se me cayó el vaso; Se me olvidó llamar. The verb agrees with the thing affected, not that person: Se me cayeron las llaves. This often presents an accident or lapse without making the affected person the grammatical subject.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 141–160, open to correction.

accidental-se.chip: se me cayó; se me olvidó
accidental-se.short: se plus an affected-person pronoun accompanies the event: Se me cayó el vaso. Match the verb to the thing: Se me cayeron las llaves. With an infinitive as subject, use singular: Se me olvidó llamar.

diminutive.name: Diminutives: smallness and affection
diminutive.about: Endings such as -ito, -ita and -cito can express small size, affection or a softer request: una casita, un cafecito, un momentito. The meaning depends on context; cafecito need not mean a smaller serving. These examples keep the gender of their base nouns.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 181–200, open to correction.

diminutive.short: Use natural diminutives in context: casita can mean little house, cafecito can sound friendly, and un momentito softens a wait. Do not add the ending to every noun.
